output:
Subject: The Saint-Hubert building — please read this

Denis,

I am writing in English so your wife can read it too, and so there is no confusion later about what I said. I have started this email more than once. I am angry. I am trying to write it straight. I am going to say everything, because if I don’t, I will say it worse on the phone.

On Thursday morning at six o’clock I was in the back shaping the baguettes. A stranger walks into my shop with a camera. He tells me he is from the agency. He says Mr. Denis told him I was okay with it. Okay with what? With a photographer walking into my bakery at six in the morning, while my hands are in the dough, to take pictures for a sale I did not know about? My employee Karine had to calm me. She had her hand on my arm. I was shaking. That is how I found out my brother put the building on the market. From a stranger with a camera.

The building is a three-storey on rue Saint-Hubert. Papa bought it in 1979. Bakery downstairs, two apartments up. Since Maman died in February, it is half yours and half mine. The estate was settled in August. I pay rent of $2,400 a month to the estate. I have never been late. Not once. In 2019 I paid $38,000 myself for the new roof. Myself. Because it is my bakery and I thought it was our building.

Then a listing appears with an agent at $1,150,000. I found it online on Centris. After. Not from you. You did not call me. You did not write me. You used an agent to tell me. I am going to say it plainly: that is a coward’s way. I am not saying you are a coward. I am saying what you did was cowardly. There is a difference, and I need you to hear it.

After Maman’s funeral you called me. You said, “No rush. We decide together.” Together. I have been holding on to those words. In September I told you on the phone I wanted to buy your half. The caisse pre-approved me for $410,000. I know that is not half of $1,150,000. I am not stupid. But it is real money from a real bank, and it is me. It keeps the building in the family. It keeps the bakery alive. You never said no. You never said anything. You just put it on the market behind my back.

My lease finishes 30 April 2027. If a developer buys, they will tear it down or make condos and double the rent. I cannot survive that. Six employees depend on me. Thirty-one years of clients come through that door. You think I am sentimental. I am. But it is business too. I get up at four in the morning. I pay my rent. I pay my salaries. I paid for the roof. The bakery is not a hobby. It is my life, and it is their jobs.

And when we were kids, Papa let you sleep in the flour sacks room in the back. You loved it. That building is not just a number on Centris. It is where we grew up. It is where Maman came downstairs with her coat still on. It is where Papa stood by the oven. I am not asking you to be sentimental. I am asking you to remember that this is not only an asset. It is our family. It is my shop. It is my employees. It is thirty-one years of clients who know my name.

Make no mistake: I am furious. I am furious that you went behind my back. I am furious that a photographer was in my shop before I had my apron on. I am furious that you let me hear it from someone else. I am furious that you said “we decide together” and then you decided alone. You are in Calgary. I am here, in the shop, every morning. Do you understand what that was like?

But I do not hate you. I am furious with you. There is a difference. I do not want to lose my brother over a building. I am writing this because I do not want to lose my brother. But I am not going to lose my bakery and my employees and thirty-one years of work without a fight either.

So here is what I want. Take the listing off the market this week. If you will not do that, then give me a first right to buy, in writing, before anyone else. I want an answer by phone, from you, not by text from your wife. I want to hear your voice. I want you to hear mine. Not a text. Not a message passed through someone else. You call me.

I am still your sister. But right now I am also the woman who has been baking in that building for thirty-one years, and I am not going to be quiet about this.

Call me. This week.

Your sister,
[Your name]
